title: ‘I’m Not MAGA,’ Says Man in MAGA Hat
summary: Elon Musk doesn’t know where people got the idea that he’s MAGA. “I’m not MAGA,” he said in an interview yesterday. “I’m not sure what MAGA means.” He went on to describe himself as “ideologically quite moderate” and added, “I don’t think I have, like, any kind of extreme political views.”This is th...
content:
Elon Musk doesn’t know where people got the idea that he’s MAGA. “I’m not MAGA,” he said in an interview yesterday. “I’m not sure what MAGA means.” He went on to describe himself as “ideologically quite moderate” and added, “I don’t think I have, like, any kind of extreme political views.”

This is the same Elon Musk who last year took the stage at the Conservative Political Action Conference wearing a black MAGA hat and wielding a chainsaw, has opined that “whites are a rapidly dying minority,” called the left “the party of murder,” posted that he loves Donald Trump “as much as a straight man can love another man,” spearheaded the Trump administration’s DOGE initiative, was the largest individual donor to Republicans in the past two elections, and just two weeks ago urged his 240 million–plus followers to “Vote red today!” on the social-media platform that he bought to wage war on the “woke mind virus.”

The world’s richest man, it seems, has changed his tune. The nearly half a billion dollars that he spent supporting Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms? That was aimed only at ensuring “checks and balances” in government, he said onstage at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit yesterday. After the historic Democratic landslide, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO is trying to do what corporate executives often do: adjust their politics to align with the party in power. Mark Zuckerberg banned Trump from Facebook after the Capitol riot on January 6, 2021; four years later, he was standing alongside Trump on the inauguration dais. Palantir CEO Alex Karp donated $1 million to a pro-Trump PAC in December 2024; last week, he told Politico that he’s a lifelong Democrat and that Palantir’s products are “essentially progressive.”

Musk’s conversion might be the least convincing yet. It’s tricky enough for a chameleon like Zuckerberg to mold his politics to the moment; most Republicans didn’t buy him as a dripped-out, flag-waving, mixed-martial-arts fan any more than most Democrats bought Facebook’s “pivot to privacy” in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica data-harvesting scandal. Musk pitching the public on his new persona as a buttoned-down centrist is like Senator Elizabeth Warren starring in a Cybertruck commercial.

Musk was not always a right-winger. He has said in the past that he voted for Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Joe Biden. His public swerve to the right began during the coronavirus pandemic and fed on his growing resentments about lockdown policies, transgender rights, and the Biden administration’s exclusion of Tesla from a White House event promoting electric vehicles. He moved from California to Texas in 2020, complaining about regulatory burdens, and brought his companies with him.

After going all-in on the GOP, Musk now figures to be among the top targets for investigation by a Democrat-led Congress. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts posted on Election Day. And Musk’s business empire is in the awkward position of relying on government contracts and regulatory approvals that will be controlled by political leaders whose party and values he has demonized. Nowhere is this problem more acute for Musk than in his adopted home state of Texas, where the Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico defeated the Republicans he had backed for governor and the Senate, respectively. Both had campaigned against Musk and data centers. (Musk did not respond to a request for comment.)

In the past, Musk has criticized politicians who publicly challenged him. When Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon called for a billionaire tax in 2021, he replied with typical delicacy: “Why does ur pp look like u just came?” Since the midterms, however, Musk has exercised uncharacteristic restraint, especially with Hinojosa, who will soon have leverage over not only data centers but also a major planned expansion of SpaceX’s Starbase, Musk’s massive Terafab semiconductor project, and the appointment of judges to the state’s business courts. Two days after the election, he shared a post characterizing Hinojosa’s approach to data centers as “reasonable” and praising her as “a political talent.” That same week, Hinojosa requested a pause on the state’s consideration of a major land sale to SpaceX until she takes office, in January. “We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms,” she said in a CNN interview. Yesterday, Musk reiterated his openness to working with Hinojosa, whom he called by her first name. “Based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said.

Mockable as Musk’s pivot might be, there’s a strategic logic to it that doesn’t depend on anyone actually believing that he’s sincere. He made the comments at a conference aimed at business insiders, investors, and policy makers. Tesla and SpaceX stocks took a hit from the midterm results, and Musk has a long history of temporarily pulling back from partisanship when he feels that his business interests are vulnerable. Investors probably don’t care as much about Musk’s politics as they care whether he remains capable of making that trade-off when needed. Musk has floated merging SpaceX and Tesla into one conglomerate, which would require approval from shareholders. And then there are the Democratic politicians Musk hopes to appease at least enough to keep his federal contacts and push through key business deals. Here, too, he doesn’t need them to believe in his conversion. He just needs to signal that he’s open to finding some common ground. Many politicians, after all, recognize the value of malleability in service of expediency.

Musk’s moderation might well prove short-lived if Democrats don’t respond the way he hopes. (After Musk’s comments yesterday, Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona posted on X: “You are still getting a subpoena.”) Regardless, his sudden circumspection suggests that something significant has already shifted: People watch their words only when they fear consequences. For two years, staying on Trump’s good side was a guarantee of protection for Musk, freeing him to say and do whatever else he wanted. That sense of impunity no longer holds.

title: The Limits of Positive Thinking
summary: As anxious Americans dealt with a cascade of computer failures over the past week, Donald Trump offered this advice: “Relax.”The air-traffic-control system, email providers, banks, airlines, and even the internal communications system of the country’s biggest intelligence agency had all seen outages...
content:
As anxious Americans dealt with a cascade of computer failures over the past week, Donald Trump offered this advice: “Relax.”

The air-traffic-control system, email providers, banks, airlines, and even the internal communications system of the country’s biggest intelligence agency had all seen outages, fueling fears of digital conspiracy. But they weren’t connected, the president assured Fox News. And hackers were not behind the outages, he insisted, because no one would dare risk retaliation by the United States. Companies were simply replacing outdated equipment, “and things happen when you put in new equipment,” he said. There was nothing to see here, no cause for alarm. “Everything’s good.”

Digital-security experts are not nearly so sanguine. They see something new and potentially ominous that’s fueling these hugely disruptive outages: artificial intelligence. Companies haven’t been replacing old equipment so much as rapidly patching newly discovered flaws in their systems with the help of sophisticated AI that can quickly spot vulnerabilities.

And why are companies moving so fast? Because attackers have AI too. The FBI warned this week about an AI-enabled tool set, called ARTEX, that “cybercriminals and state-aligned hackers” are using to identify weakness and develop attacks in under three hours. None of the affected companies has said that it thinks its systems went down because of an attack. But security experts told us that in the past few weeks, they have been struggling to keep up with an onslaught of attempted hacks from AI-enabled adversaries. And rushing to harden lots of computer infrastructure all at once can be messy and inconsistent, explaining some of the disruptions.

Trump has never fully reckoned with the risks of AI. He prefers to call it “superintelligence,” an odd choice given that that’s the term some doomsayers use for AI that becomes self-aware and tries to wipe out humanity. The president frames the race to develop advanced AI as an existential contest between China and the United States. “Whoever wins AI wins,” he is fond of saying. The Defense Department has deployed AI systems across its networks with seemingly little regard for the risks of using them in combat. Trump has avoided creating safety regulations and guardrails and has followed the counsel of executives whose fortunes depend on AI expansion. That includes ex–Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has consistently downplayed the risk of out-of-control AI, calling apocalyptic scenarios “made-up” or baseless.

When it comes to developing and deploying the technology, Trump is all gas and no brakes.

For a different president, the nerve-racking outages of the past week might have been a moment for sober reflection on whether the United States is prepared for what’s coming. Even some Republicans are asking for that, as are some Democrats. “It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, a Democrat who is in line to chair the Senate Intelligence Committee in the next Congress, said in a statement. Warner has proposed legislation that would subject AI models to greater scrutiny and safety checks. “Americans deserve clear, reliable information and a government that is prepared to respond,” Warner said.

But the administration seems not to grasp how worried many Americans are at suddenly being unable to check their bank balance or read their email. The disappearance of everyday conveniences comes after months of dark warnings about rogue AI agents and renewed fears of cyberattacks from Iran. The French government publicly accused Iran last week of remotely sabotaging food-refrigeration units and causing mass spoilage in grocery stores. Trump may insist that there’s nothing to be concerned about, but even some of his allies fear that something bigger is at play. “If this is all a coincidence,” Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, a Republican, told reporters on Tuesday, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.”

Normally, in the middle of a domestic crisis, an administration tries to speak with one voice and tell a coherent story to an anxious public. But as bank websites crashed at the same time as stranded passengers slept in airports, no one in the administration seemed to know what was happening or who was in charge of fixing things.

On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who is supposed to lead the government’s response to domestic cybersecurity incidents, suggested that artificial intelligence deployed on computer networks was “self-fixing itself.” In the scenario he described, recent network collapses were the result of a big, messy patching job. That is close to what experts think is continuing to happen. But Mullin attributed his understanding to a tech leader, whom he declined to name, telling Fox News that his theory “kind of makes sense.” This uncertain description, from an official with access to an array of classified government intelligence and seasoned briefers, did little to allay concerns.

[Read: The secretary of imprecision]

The unit within Mullin’s department that should be running point in this crisis, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has lost almost a third of its 3,200 employees since Trump returned to office two years ago. The White House wants to cut the budget for some agency programs, including election security, by $700 million next year. When we went to the CISA website today, we found guidance about recent incidents, forms for reporting cyberattacks, and a two-month-old handbook for “Communicating Under Pressure.”

“During service outages, clear communication matters,” CISA unironically advised.

Officials dismissed any connection between the computer failures and the deep staffing and budget cuts at the agency. “The implication that the recent events would not have occurred if CISA had more employees is patently false,” a White House official said.

The new director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, told a congressional committee yesterday that “the timing of these ​incidents can raise questions, ​and it should,” but he insisted that the outages were coincidental and “associated with maintenance and ​technical ​changes.” Clayton also blamed the patching of vulnerabilities, but he didn’t blame AI.

Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and the national security adviser, appeared initially confused when a reporter asked at a press conference in Manila whether AI had played a role in the outages. He said he couldn’t confirm that that was the case but explained why AI hypothetically could have led to the systems failing. Rubio stressed that “people are fearful; people are uncertain” and said that it was important for the administration to “share with them transparently what we know.”

Trump’s habit, when he is confronted with a crisis, is to rely on the power of positive thinking. In the first weeks of 2020, he was slow to sound the alarm on a new virus discovered in China, reportedly for fear of rattling financial markets and upsetting Xi Jinping. By the time he left office a year later, some 400,000 people in the United States had died of COVID-19. A similar dynamic now seems to be at work. Trump has resisted calls even from within the AI industry to regulate the technology, fearing that government interference will stymie innovation and slow growth. The president knows that AI companies are propping up the stock market and that U.S. economic expansion depends largely on the construction of new data centers, which are essential for developing more powerful AI models.

Trump was in China this week for meetings with Xi and Vladimir Putin, and he indicated to allies that he didn’t want anything to distract from those sessions. That could explain the at-times-nonexistent messaging from the White House. During the height of Friday’s ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration—which does not appear to have been caused by AI-related patching—Trump was huddled in the Oval Office with the actor Jon Voight, talking about Hollywood tax rebates. He stayed out of sight for days, leaving Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to make a widely panned series of appearances in which they largely blamed the Biden administration and demanded money from Congress. One air traffic controller told us that everything he and his colleagues had learned about the nationwide ground stop—an event that has happened only three times this century—came from the same general announcement Duffy had made to the public. The controller said that he had received no information internally about the outage and its causes.

Officials privately acknowledge that an extraordinary amount of work needs to be done to fend off the relentless and increasing AI attacks. But the president’s advisers may be wary of telling the public the truth about the scale of the threat because they don’t want to make Trump angry, two Republicans close to the White House told us on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations.

[Read: Trump sets the olive branch on fire]

In his Fox News interview, Trump said that journalists were exploiting the computer crashes for political purposes: “The press is sort of having a lot of fun with it. If these things would’ve happened two years ago, three years ago, in the Biden administration, which was grossly incompetent and corrupt, nobody would’ve mentioned it.” Journalists extensively covered similar breakdowns, including a nationwide ground stop in 2023 and the discovery of a massive penetration of U.S. telecom networks by China, through an actor known as Salt Typhoon, the following year.

Trump insisted on Fox News that the weeklong parade of cyber horribles was a mere coincidence. “I’ll let you know if there’s a problem,” he said.

After the past week, the bar for what Trump considers to be a problem is looking awfully high.

Isaac Stanley-Becker and Madison Hahamy contributed to this article.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI Is Really Weird
summary: Jason Duval lives in a shack on the Leonida Keys, in the simulated Florida where Grand Theft Auto VI is set. I began playing the game after its release at midnight, and I have already tried and failed to outrun the police, roamed the hallways of a prison, driven a speedboat to collect cocaine droppe...
content:
Jason Duval lives in a shack on the Leonida Keys, in the simulated Florida where Grand Theft Auto VI is set. I began playing the game after its release at midnight, and I have already tried and failed to outrun the police, roamed the hallways of a prison, driven a speedboat to collect cocaine dropped by a seaplane pilot who was skimming from a more upmarket criminal, and flown the seaplane to escape an RV park full of wild-animal-and-narcotics traffickers.

If you know anything at all about the game, which almost 5,000 people worked on for more than a decade at a reported cost of more than $1 billion, it is that Leonida is enormous. Early reviewers are bragging on social media about spending more than 100 hours in the world of the game, while only scratching the surface of what is possible. The prospect seems overwhelming because I already have a life that requires labor and demands diversion, and I am worried about how to fit GTA VI’s simulated work and recreation into my supposedly real life.

Theorists of video games (a real thing that I could be accused of being) have a name for this phenomenon: playbor, a portmanteau of play and labor. Many jobs feel fake now anyway—“email jobs,” they were scornfully called even before AI could be mustered to carry out their pointlessness—and games feel like jobs, with a seemingly endless list of menial tasks for their players.

[Read: The least productive day of the year]

An hour or so in, though, the game offers a breather to look around and get your bearings. I decide to stay in Jason’s house instead of venturing out into even a tiny corner of Leonida. There is so much to do here that I find myself wondering how many hours I might spend indoors, inside the pretend home of a fake man. After all, I pass most of my own life as a real man inside my real home, working and puttering, instead of exploring the city or countryside that contain me.

Jason has a pet snake, and walking by its glass habitat triggers a text overlay indicating that I can interact with it. I press a button to feed the snake, and Jason reaches into a blue plastic container, carefully retrieves a mouse, and drops it into the cage. I can see another mouse or two in there, of varied shades. I already feel as though I need to resupply the snake food. I find myself wondering where one goes for snake mice, and what that shop might be called in Grand Theft Auto.

“Thoughtful actions will increase your focus bar,” the game tells me after I feed the animal. Feeding a snake is thoughtful, apparently. A purple icon animates and a corresponding purple bar fills slightly to communicate the effect of the act. Jason’s stamina and strength are also measured in health-bar form. Some games allocate a bar for hunger or even bladder level.

This kind of thing used to seem ridiculous, a perverse way to understand human behavior for the nerds who design and play video games. But when I look at my real smartwatch on my actual wrist, I realize the world has caught up. It translates my movement into a number on a red bar that supposedly represents my activity. I don’t believe that the numbers—383 calories so far today—are real, but I orient my activities around them every day. Better do a quick Peloton to close my rings; time for another walk to get my steps in. I don’t think about it much anymore, but I have become a video-game avatar of myself.

In the shack, morning light pours across a desk from a window whose blinds are raised halfway. On the desk are a radio, a few books, and a conch shell. You know that a video-game object is relevant when it receives an overlay with a text description and an icon of the controller button used to interact with it. In this case, the radio’s channels can be changed with a button on my PlayStation 5 controller, and the book can be examined with a different button. I cannot interact with the conch.

After flipping to a station called Afrobank FM, I examine the book. It’s called Orca: A Whole Different Animal. The book isn’t about killer whales. It’s a send-up of the Navy SEALs and the kind of inspirational title that a former officer might write as CEO of a private mercenary firm or in anticipation of running for a U.S. Senate seat. I can open the book, which contains actual text on simulated pages.

I’ve read that Rockstar Games, the creator of GTA, did not use generative AI during the production of the game, and instead employs a large team of people who create all of the media inside it—including Orca, presumably. I wonder whether libraries or bookstores exist in the game, which I might then treat as a laborious literary experience rather than a criminal-underworld fantasy. But flipping through Orca reveals that the game surfaces only a few pages. The book is not real, in the sense that a book contains writing sufficient to justify a book. It is, instead, an icon of a book, like the conch is an icon for decor. I somewhat wish that Rockstar had used AI to generate books instead. I assume—I haven’t looked yet—that someone has, by now, generated a real, fake version of Orca: A Whole Different Animal and put it up for sale on Amazon.

Jason’s eyes suggest an earnestness that makes me want to like him. The hairs at the top of the mustache stick out and up slightly, in a casual manner that suggests affability more than unkemptness. It seems remarkable to be able to interpret a character in this way, and I find myself suspicious of the matter. Not too long ago, an “uncanny valley” effect made computer characters seem unreal—they were immensely real but just shy of credible, and that gap made them slightly creepy. The gap appears to have been closed.

Now, instead, I wonder whether I really like Jason or am being tricked into liking him by how well the game has established his plight. Earlier, he hooked up with Lucia Caminos, the game’s other protagonist, whom I had controlled as she committed a robbery that got her arrested. I’ve watched Jason tolerate a prolix conspiracy theorist named Cal and rescue a hot-mess smuggler named Donnie. His ex-military credentials have been established, and Jason’s all-American appearance suggests a good guy in a bad spot. The writing and characterization are good in the way a television show is these days—which is to say, too good, too clean. The paradox of fiction has become the new hurdle. I find myself worrying that my years of vocal skepticism about video-game storytelling are at risk of coming undone.

When uncanniness persists, it offers me comfort. In the kitchen, I can make Jason pour a coffee and drink it. Doing so raises his focus and his stamina, as coffee is known to do. He drinks it so quickly that I worry about scalding him, but that is tempered by the realization that he didn’t really drink it—no liquid moves between the mug’s lip and Jason’s mouth, as if the mug had been a prop in a black-box theater production or a stop-motion animation. The simplest background acts of other narrative media, such as films or novels, require enormous amounts of engineering to accomplish in software. In a book, you can say, “Jason poured and drank a cup of coffee.” In a movie, you can point the camera at an actor doing so, and the act along with the liquid’s heat shimmer would be captured through the lens. But nothing is free in games.

Jason continues holding the mug as I walk around his place. It dangles from his right hand like a cigarette. When he opens the fridge at the behest of a button press, he does so with his nonpreferred hand, so he can continue clinging to the mug. The game interprets the mug in the same way it would a pistol—an object is probably a weapon, one that you’d want to put down only deliberately.

If I let go of the controller, Jason enters what game developers call an idle state. It would seem weird if a game simply stopped when the player isn’t doing something, so the software makes the characters bob and sway in a manner that seems realistic until it goes on too long. Jason’s body moves to the beat of the music on Afrobank FM, in this case “Tomorrow,” by Ntombi Ndaba, a real South African singer from the late 1980s. GTA often does this, mixing mocking or fictional media with licensed ones in a way that makes you doubt whether you know which element is real and which is invented. That feeling accompanies every moment of life today, because the internet is full of lies that might also be true. Idle Jason nodded his fictional head along to the real Ntombi Ndaba in his fictional Leonida tank top, as if to agree with me.

Some of my colleagues in writing and academia—the ones who hate artificial intelligence—have taken to the idea that “writing is thinking.” They use this shorthand as a self-evident takedown of AI. If people had to write (well, presumably?) to think, then nobody would ever think—especially academics. I have to walk to think, so I put down the PlayStation controller to take a walk to try to figure out what I think about Grand Theft Auto VI.

After you have played a video game, the real world feels more akin to the apparatus you control in a video game. My feet no longer felt like my own as they crunched gravel on the street. Construction is everywhere in my neighborhood, the consequence of a tornado that blew through here 18 months ago. I steered my human body around a hole in the pavement and a construction dumpster at the gutter. A worker was standing between the sidewalk and an approaching pickup truck, and I had to veer uncomfortably close to him to get by.

As I did, I inhaled the strong smell of his cologne, which vanished as quickly as it appeared. You cannot smell in Grand Theft Auto, a game for the eyes and ears and thumbs. This somehow made smelling seem unimportant, rather than making the game feel insufficiently realistic. The construction worker’s cologne came across as improbable and fake.

A wardrobe in the corner allows me to change Jason out of his tank top and into other garments—a military outfit, workout wear, pajamas. I switch to swimwear, and the game previews Jason in red trunks and no shirt.

I find myself studying his body in distressing detail. I’ve been working out seriously for the past two years or so and become occasionally concerned about the tone of my abs, a vanity I find embarrassing to admit. Along the way, I’ve worried that the AI depictions of the human body on YouTube fitness-video previews are giving me body dysmorphia. Jason’s abs look as toned (or less?) than mine, which I had checked in the mirror this morning. This fact makes me feel somehow affirmed—that I am in as good of shape as an animated video-game antihero.

A triangle appears in Jason’s bathroom, indicating that I can shower. Doing so cuts to a shot of Jason from behind, his naked ass visible under the flowing water. Nudity feels like an attempt to make a video game serious in the way that it once did for cable-television shows. The whole idea has been prudishly outmoded on TV; there, visible vomiting indicates seriousness rather than butts or boobs.

[Ian Bogost: Zelda’s midlife crisis]

I can make Jason shower, after a fashion. You pull a trigger on the controller to scrub and, while doing so, use the left joystick to move his hands. Driving is like this too—akin to piloting a vehicle, if a vehicle were a marionette instead of a machine. Getting clean increases Jason’s focus. When he emerges from the shower (hold a button to dress), Jason is still carrying the coffee mug.

Years ago, I took my son to the empty parking lot of a local shopping mall to teach him to drive. He struggled with hand-over-hand steering, because video games had given him a false idea about the process of driving a vehicle. Driving in video games has always overstated the sensitivity of steering. (A few years later, my daughter, who had played only Nintendo’s Animal Crossing, had no such trouble.)

Jason drives a beat-up Chevy El Camino, which is fictionalized as the Cheval Picador in the series. Although GTA has always encouraged reckless driving, I had heard that you have to be more careful in this game, because you need to repair your car if it gets damaged, and that requires money, which demands in-game work. But the game frustrated my attempts to drive properly, as if the ghosts of its prior iterations were haunting the new doctrine of vehicular realism. Backing up has always been a freak show in GTA, and I immediately blew out a taillight.

When I regained composure, I found myself commuting, for real. I kept two car lengths back in traffic. I stopped at stop signs in the middle of nowhere. I took turns wide and felt guilty when my perception of the road, unaided by the embodiment that would make real driving easy, caused me to mistake an oncoming lane for my own. When I arrived at Jason’s house, where the map had guided me, I accidentally pulled into a neighboring property. It was night and hard to see. I felt guilty, the way you do when your Uber from the airport pulls into a neighbor’s driveway instead of your own.

Years ago, a less adept game with similarly adult ambitions, called Heavy Rain, allowed the player to intervene in narrative cutscenes via a technique known as quick-time events. Early on, the player loses track of a child named Jason in a mall. This failure turns tragic and motivates the rest of the story (which is, alas, stupid). The game instructs the player, who is frantically searching for Jason, to press “X” to call out for him. This mortifying depiction of human terror became a meme, at a time when memes were still new: “Press X to Jason.”

Surely, it is no accident that one of the main characters in GTA VI is also named Jason. Pressing “X” to Jason has finally grown up, not because the act is more serious but because the world has acclimated to it. Press “X” to dinner in DoorDash. Press “X” to time off in Workday. Press “X” to health care in MyChart.

Someone told me that they heard Grand Theft Auto VI begins with a lot of cutscenes. That is not quite right. It begins with paperwork. Accept the license agreement. Affirm the privacy policy. Choose your heads-up-display design. Calibrate the brightness and color gamut of your monitor. Enable subtitles or select on-screen-text size. Games such as this one have longed to meet or replace Hollywood films for decades. In some ways, they have.

In others, the reverse has taken place. Watching television or cinema—which one does at home now, principally—involves operating software services as much as consuming media: scrolling menus, running updates, scanning QR codes to log in.

The French theorist Jean Baudrillard knew about the future—our present—decades before time revealed it to you and me. Everything would become simulation, a barrage of representation replacing lived reality. These were ideas, complex and hard-to-read ones. Baudrillard also anticipated the form of the internet age, with its short bursts of disconnected meaning. He wrote many books entirely from aphorisms, including one about America (called America) and a series on anything he could think of (called Cool Memories). Just as the photographer Stephen Shore accidentally invented Instagram in the 1970s, so Baudrillard accidentally invented Twitter in the 1980s.

Two weeks ago, culling some of the many books in my office, I donated a couple boxes of ’80s and ’90s theory that felt irrelevant today. But I kept America and Cool Memories. I have always yearned to write like that, like Baudrillard, in aphorism rather than argument. GTA VI finally justified it, by turning life (or its simulation) into a series of disconnected rituals.

I have to make a disclosure. Take-Two Interactive, the company that owns Rockstar Games, the creator of GTA VI, has paid me a lot of money over the years for legal consulting related to intellectual-property litigation.

One of those cases involved the parent company’s sports games, such as the NBA 2K series, made by the Take-Two subsidiary 2K Games. A tattoo artist had sued Take-Two for reproducing the tattoos he had inked on LeBron James’s actual body, which he claimed the game developer needed permission to reproduce in virtual form, despite the fact that 2K Games had secured the rights to James’s (and every other NBA player’s) likeness via an agreement with the NBA. The realism of the games was central to the dispute.

[Listen: Will the new Grand Theft Auto be a weapon in the culture wars?]

During the trial’s testimony, the opposing counsel showed me a version of NBA 2K that his litigation team had configured to play with two teams composed entirely of LeBron Jameses. “Is this realistic?” the attorney challenged. “Yes,” I responded. What he showed amounted to a realistic depiction of what reality would look like were you to stage a professional basketball game composed entirely of James clones.

Take-Two won the case.

Out on Jason’s deck, ring marks on the wooden railing caps look like they have been painted on rather than worn in as moisture. When I look across the swampy bog surrounding the house, everything is too bright. The shadows don’t look dark enough, and the highlights appear too washed out. It looks like a high-dynamic-range computer rendering.

Or it did, before the software in smartphones, which are the devices people now use to take photographs, started performing intensive processing, including high dynamic range. That’s why what you see in the world tends to look deep-fried in your pictures. That style is now so commonplace that it has become what a photograph looks like—what the world looks like, once it is shared as photographs on social media.

There, looking across the HDR water of the Leonida Keys, I held a button on the controller to put down the mug Jason was still holding. He set it on the wood railing cap overlooking the swamp. There, the software gave it a label, Mug, and a triangle icon indicating that I could pick it up again.

title: I Baked My Way Through The Atlantic’s Archives
summary: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.The most cherished recipes are usually the hardest to follow. They live on stained index cards and notes worn thin at the creases, in handwriting so faded you have to squ...
content:
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.

The most cherished recipes are usually the hardest to follow. They live on stained index cards and notes worn thin at the creases, in handwriting so faded you have to squint to read it. That handwriting belongs to a grandmother or a distant relative, and it was meant for someone who already knew the dish: Add a pinch of this, a teacup of that; bake until done.

I’ve spent a lot of time in The Atlantic’s archives, and I kept running into such recipes tucked into letters, essays, and memoirs, rarely where you’d expect them. I was curious to know whether they still work—and, more important, how they taste. The further back I went, the less my finds looked like recipes. They read like stories, and you had to read closely to find the instructions.

Take this “Letter to a Young Housekeeper,” from November 1865, written by C. P. Hawes to “M.,” a bride newly married to “H.” Hawes spends most of the letter arguing that cooking is a fine art and a science, which the woman of the house should learn for herself. She is funny about it, and a little grand. Recalling one early success at the table, Hawes reaches for Henry David Thoreau, whose essays had recently run in this magazine, to describe the dishes: “We ate, lingered, and revelled in them, thus becoming epicures at once … They were as great a revelation to the palate as Bettine or Thoreau might be to the mind.”

Only at the very end does she mention a “well-tested” recipe for bread: a quart of milk, a teacup of “hopyeast,” and enough flour “to make it quite stiff.” How much flour? How hot an oven? And how long does it bake for? Hawes doesn’t say.

For much of history, recipes moved from one cook to another by word of mouth and by experience: watching a mother at the stove, having a neighbor ask for a missing ingredient. Cookbooks didn’t exist simply because, for centuries, most women couldn’t read, Sarah Lohman, a culinary historian, told me. As literacy spread in the 18th century, women began keeping handwritten notes of family recipes to pass down or to copy for a daughter when she was married. Those recipes were light on instructions by design. They expected you to rely on your instincts “to know when the batter looks right or to know when the cake is done,” Lohman said.

By the early 20th century, written recipes had become something to amass, and cookbooks were treated as literature. “It was with something of a shock that I woke one morning and found myself a collector of cookery books,” the American writer Elizabeth Robins Pennell wrote in The Atlantic in 1901. What she prized most were the traces that earlier owners of the books left behind.

Her copy of The Queen-Like Closet, a 17th-century cookbook by Hannah Woolley, had several owners before it reached her—one of whom was a young woman named Mary Halfpenny, who had received it as a gift in 1678 and went on to add her own recipes to its pages. A century later, another family used it as their “Bible,” recording their children’s births in the margins. Pennell loved those scribbles: “They add a distinctly personal charm to the shabby little old cookery book.” And sometimes, the actual Bible held recipes too. In 1910, a writer in this magazine’s Contributors’ Club described the family Bible as a place where you might find anything tucked between the pages, from a father’s old report cards “to mother’s recipe for sponge-cake.”

But around midcentury, the American recipe changed shape, in part due to technology. I asked Lohman why some of the 19th-century recipes I’d baked didn’t call for butter or eggs. Before the advent of the refrigerator, Lohman explained, these ingredients were seasonal: Cows give milk after calving, from late winter into summer, and hens tend to take a break from laying in winter. Sure enough, the 19th-century recipes missing those ingredients were fall and winter dishes. By the mid-1950s, the majority of American homes had a refrigerator.

As kitchens changed, recipes changed with them: more exact, more complete, easier for a stranger to follow. But the story behind the food has never quite gone away. Even as recipes grew more precise and the ingredients in them stopped shifting with the seasons, the people who wrote them kept reaching for memories. In 1985, Corby Kummer, then an editor at The Atlantic, began an essay on pie not with flour or butter but with a tale about his mother’s pie crust, an unforgettable taste that “has driven me to pursue the elusive art of making pastry.”

And as recipes moved online, the stories came with them. Food blogs, and later videos, wrapped their instructions in anecdotes; anyone who has looked up a recipe on their phone knows the feeling of scrolling past several paragraphs of backstory before the ingredient list appears. Some of that is less sentimental than it seems (long blocks of text help a recipe rank higher in search results and make more room for ads). Still, it is telling that when food writers have space to fill, they fill it with stories.

I have been baking since I was a child, learning from my mother and grandmothers and from recipes handed down for generations. I was curious whether the recipes I found from over the decades still hold up today. So I baked my way through the archives, beginning with Hawes’s 1865 biscuits and ending on a batch of brownies from 2010. Where an ingredient or instruction was missing, I filled in what I thought each recipe left out and made my best guess about certain directions (what it means to age in a tin, or to roll to “exactly the right thickness”). The recipes below are adapted from the originals, based on my own testing (I’ve indicated any discrepancies with the original recipes by adding “modified” to the ingredients list). Here’s what happened—and my honest assessment of how it all tasted.

Biscuits, 1865

In C. P. Hawes’s Atlantic story, she promises her dough will make “two small loaves and a half-dozen biscuits.” What came out of my oven were plain dinner rolls, and only about a dozen (there was no dough left for the loaves). Today’s biscuits are made with butter; Hawes’s dough is mostly milk, flour, and yeast. And not the yeast we buy now. Home bakers used to make their own, often by brewing it with hops. Hawes calls for a teacup of this so-called hop yeast—I used a packet of active dry yeast instead.

The result: a simple bread roll with a slightly floury taste. Not quite a Thoreau-level revelation. But if you want a very simple dinner roll for the table, this is the recipe for you. (And if you’re after a tall, fluffy biscuit, Amanda Mull cracked the code in 2018.)

Apple Dowdy, 1936

The cook and writer Della T. Lutes, whose Atlantic essays became part of her award-winning 1936 book, The Country Kitchen, calls her Apple Dowdy “a homely dish,” and she wasn’t being modest. A cross between an apple pie and an apple cobbler, mine came out of the oven looking exactly as advertised. At first, I wondered whether the Dowdy came before the pie, but not quite: Sarah Lohman told me that by the end of the 18th century, pies were “pretty much how they are today.” The pandowdy is just a less fussy way to get to a similar place.

Lutes gives no quantities at all—she just writes that the dish needs a deep bed of sliced, spiced, buttered apples under a thick crust, baked “at least an hour, very slowly.”

The result: a slightly watery dessert that isn’t the prettiest, but tastes decent. The consistency of the filling needed improvement, and it also could have used more flavor (I’d recommend going heavier on the spice).

Lebkuchen, 1949

In 1949, the cookbook author Virginia Pasley described a holiday tradition that began with a search. Her mother “tried recipe after recipe” for Lebkuchen, a spiced German honey cookie, “like Mother used to make.” The Lebkuchen that finally passed the test came from Mrs. Schmidt next door. The writer and her siblings, who wanted to help, were allowed only to sliver the almonds and cut up the citron. Now I understand why. The recipe calls for so much honey that it ended up all over my kitchen, and stirring the stiff dough with 9(!) cups of flour was an arm workout. 

The result: This one was divisive among my taste-testers. The Lebkuchen is dense and very chewy, a workout for your jaw too. But if you like something not too sweet or soft to dunk in tea, this could be your cookie.

Apple pie, 1985 and 2009

For this one, I paired two recipes from two eras. The crust comes from Corby Kummer, who opens his 1985 essay dismissing store-bought crust as tasting “like the box it came in.” His own recipe is the opposite: flaky, rich, and well worth the effort. The filling is from Ezekiel Emanuel’s 2009 apple-crisp recipe, which was helpful enough to provide me with a list of ingredients, a pan size, and the oven temperature. 

Pie crust

Apple crisp filling

The result: Kummer’s crust was so good that it stood out to the people who tried it. (Store-bought just doesn’t compare to his recipe.) The filling was a big step up from Lutes’s Dowdy. Emanuel himself says his filling is “almost identical to the one for apple pie,” and that’s how it tasted: like a solid, classic apple pie. Overall, a satisfying combination of recipes.

Brownies, 2010

The newest recipe on my list comes from my colleague Eleanor Barkhorn, a senior editor at The Atlantic. It was part of a weekly series she wrote while training for a marathon. Unlike the older recipes, it leaves almost nothing to the imagination: There are eight ingredients and exact measurements. When I reached out to Eleanor, she had a few updates to the instructions: She sometimes ups the chocolate to 10 ounces, and she no longer recommends the mixer, because it can overmix the batter. Instead, she said it’s better to sift the flour onto the batter and then fold it in carefully with a spatula. 

The result: very good brownies with a perfect texture that were not hard to make. They were a favorite with my tasters. Definitely worth baking a batch.

PS

Family recipes are still finding their way into the pages of The Atlantic. For the December issue, Danyel Smith wrote about her Aunt Louise’s famous mac and cheese and the unexpected ingredient that set it apart. Does your family have a recipe like that, with a secret, a story, and one person who makes it best? I’d love to hear about it. Let us know in the comments. (We may share your answer, including your first name and last initial, age, and/or location, with fellow readers in a future edition of this newsletter or on our website or social-media platforms.)

— Rafaela

title: Silicon Valley is Suffering From Model Collapse
summary: For anyone living outside Northern California, a lot of the messages coming out of Silicon Valley feel like they’ve been sent from another planet. Last week, many of the industry’s top minds engaged in Olympic-level mental gymnastics as they defended the former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affairs: We ...
content:
For anyone living outside Northern California, a lot of the messages coming out of Silicon Valley feel like they’ve been sent from another planet. Last week, many of the industry’s top minds engaged in Olympic-level mental gymnastics as they defended the former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affairs: We must excuse his dalliances with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, they argued, not just because Huang is absolutely necessary to the American economy, which is being propped up by AI investment, but because we are in a geopolitical  superintelligence race with China.

Then this week, Anthropic, the company most vocally obsessed with the existential risk of AI, went public in an effort to raise $90 billion so that it could speed up construction of the very same systems it’s warning us about.

How do we explain this pattern of illogical behavior? Maybe it’s standard avarice: Shareholders stand to make unfathomable amounts of money from Nvidia and Anthropic stock, and, ultimately, cash rules everything around me. But many Anthropic employees seem uninterested in the money. Maybe it’s groupthink. Maybe it’s a religious-level belief in the abundance of a future in which humans have ushered in superintelligence. Or maybe it’s the cult of the founder and a messianic sense of grandeur—the conviction that only those who see the future first in San Francisco can help protect us from the scourge of disease, from the Chinese, or from ourselves.

[Read: ]A $5.7 trillion face-plant

But watching the AI doomerism on X, the lead-up to Anthropic’s IPO, and the fallout from Huang’s resignation, I think there’s a better framework for understanding what we’re seeing. The degradation of logic, the inscrutable decision making, and the bizarre detachment from popular opinion all point to a dynamic that the AI industry calls model collapse. The term describes a type of digital inbreeding that can theoretically occur when AI models train off synthetic AI output. The most influential figures in AI now sound as if they, having marinated in the insular worlds of the Bay Area and X, are suffering from their own version of the phenomenon.

Model collapse isn’t a perfect analogy. AI companies actually take pains to filter out AI slop when training their language models. But humans? Not so much. You might call it circular reasoning, but the overall takeaway is the same: The corporate leaders shaping our future seem stuck in their own world. A recent post on a popular AI blog captures this spirit well, comparing AI-company employees to people who are microdosing psychedelics. These individuals appear as if they are “in a chronically mildly altered state of mind,” the post argues. Maybe, the post suggests, this state of mind allows them to “see some things more clearly” about AI models and their progress and capabilities than those of us on the outside. The downside, of course, is some form of inebriation. This is a helpful framework through which to view a lot of what’s coming out of the Bay Area. But there’s also a compounding effect: All day, every day, this culture talks with itself, its participants training on a recursive loop of information about the world and what they are building. This information bubble is self-reinforcing, frequently illogical, and also alienating.

The Silicon Valley discourse about recursive self improvement in AI offers the best example of this degraded, circular reasoning. RSI refers to the concept of AI models improving themselves without human intervention or supervision, which would improve AI capabilities exponentially, accelerating discoveries in different fields and increasing the likelihood that models show signs of superintelligence and become far better than humans at any task they pursue. The downside of RSI, according to individuals including the Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, is that models “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.” Humans would be flying blind and thus would likely rely more heavily on AI systems to interpret what is happening inside other AI systems. This is already happening to varying degrees when AI companies train and test new models, but RSI would speed it up to the point that humans would have fully relinquished control. This prospect seems to terrify many of the people who are closest to the technology. “There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI. Please look up!” Anna Wang, an alignment researcher at Anthropic, wrote this fall.

Yet companies keep racing toward RSI out of fear that someone less principled will get there first. Anthropic argues that pushing forward with an eye toward AI safety will create a virtuous cycle of innovation—a “race to the top.” But you could just as easily argue that these companies are plowing ahead to justify and pay for hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure investments. Or that they are so deeply locked in competition with other AI companies and open models in China that they’re behaving irrationally.

This September, Amodei wrote an essay arguing for a multilateral slowdown of AI development, a process he dubbed “pacing the frontier.” Ten days later, Anthropic released its newest model. Roughly a month later, in its IPO filing, the company confessed that its call to pace the frontier “does not describe our own model development or release timelines.”

Sometimes, you can see the model collapse happening at an individual level—and it looks like naked hypocrisy. In September, an Anthropic researcher named Jacob Coxon quit the company in order to argue that AI companies might kill us all. He offered a heartfelt and convincing case in favor of taking the risk of human extinction seriously. But then, when asked in an interview that surfaced this week whether he would donate his OpenAI shares, he seemed to laugh off the suggestion that doing so would make any difference. “I like the money, bro,” he told the audience. He has since agreed to donate his equity.

Sigal Samuel, a writer who covers AI at Vox, has argued that at least some of this dynamic can be explained by a Silicon Valley culture steeped in effective altruism and rationalism. In this sphere, it’s not uncommon for adherents to justify huge risks using counterintuitive and dispassionate rationale. Some see this as a sophisticated form of argumentation, one that can eschew conventional morality (by risking rogue-AI swarm hacks or worse) for a greater purpose (achieving a technological utopia). Samuel argues that the hyperrational thinking deployed by these leaders is overly clever. “Commonsense morality is actually often commonsense for a reason,” she told me recently. “And that’s because it tracks intuitions. Usually, reasoning like ‘If you don’t want a doom machine, don’t build a doom machine’ tends to be good reasoning.”

Some who have quit the AI companies in protest describe the internal cultures as nonsensical, even schizophrenic, in nature. David Robinson, who wrote OpenAI’s transparency reports as a safety lead, argued in this publication that the company, which speaks obsessively about safety, approached AI development “with unimpeded optimism about being able to solve problems as they arise,” leading it to adopt a trial-and-error approach that is no longer responsible, given the power of its models. Relentless optimism is a necessary component of technological achievement but, as Robinson suggests, it can veer into hubris.

And so the Gordian knot grows ever tighter: Founders argue that humanity must accept enormous trade-offs for the benefit of a technological revolution. In exchange for curing cancer, one must be willing to risk the many-sided threat of gradual disempowerment, in the form of either mass job loss or a world where much of the cognitive work is performed by machines. Many of the people grinding away to usher in this future seem to lack humility or be unable to articulate whether the society they’re building toward is one that’s worth living in at all. At some point, their plainly stated claims can end up sounding, frankly, insane. Recently on X, an AI enthusiast argued that one possible positive end state for humans in an AI utopia would be that “we become the happy dogs” living in a world that “does not belong to them.” Musk has said that we might end up like a “pet Labrador if we’re lucky.” He has also argued that it is “unlikely” that humans will be in control in 10 years time. It all signals a certain irrational confidence in where the future is headed, and a disregard for how off-putting it all sounds.

To prevent model collapse, AI companies don’t just add more data to training sets; they add higher-quality information from a diverse array of sources. The dynamic, according to some research, is not an evenly distributed phenomenon, meaning that it appears in specific areas of a model where there are weak points in the training data. A natural fix is to identify the blind spots or shallow areas and bolster them with better data. If Silicon Valley followed this example, perhaps what they would find is an enormous political blind spot.

A June survey of Americans by the Pew Research Center showed that just 9 percent of respondents were more excited than concerned about AI, while 52 percent were more concerned than excited. In an exit poll from the recent midterm elections, 56 percent of voters responded that AI and data centers were a “crucial or major factor” in how they had voted. A recent survey of 1,000 young Americans suggested that few of them trust tech CEOs to act responsibly with AI. Yet many voices in Silicon Valley seem either disconnected from this reality or spiteful of it, accusing anti–data center voters of destroying America’s path to prosperity. As the fallout from the Nvidia scandal shows, Silicon Valley’s disconnect goes beyond just the general public; the venture capitalists arguing for Huang’s reinstatement seem to miss or simply not care about the bipartisan anger in Washington over Huang’s clearly reckless behavior. In an industry that has thoroughly embraced civilizational risk, the notion of the replaceable founder seems to be the true existential threat to the tech elite.

Tech executives are failing at politics for the same reason they’re struggling among regular Americans: They’ve been so monomaniacally focused on winning the AI race that they’ve ignored everything else, including the need to build consensus or even a baseline of enthusiasm for their plans. That may be why the midterm shift away from MAGA took them by surprise. Maybe it’s because they believe that nobody, outside of the AI companies, is qualified or intelligent enough to judge their work, making them both perpetually unaccountable and correct in every argument. Perhaps it is because they believe that the technology is so self-evidently powerful that a public consensus is irrelevant. That could prove to be true, but in the interim, their rhetoric comes off as incomprehensible, frequently condescending, and too often frantic.

At some point, the behaviors that signal a model collapse can also resemble those of a gambler on a bender. One day’s ecstasy over abundant superintelligence turns into the next day’s dire warnings about the future. Half of Silicon Valley appears to be arguing that AI progress is unstoppable—that human loss of control (or life) within the next year seems inevitable; the other half seems to suggest that the entire fate of both AI progress and the economy hinges on one man in a leather jacket who sells chips. Regardless, the only way out is through, so you go harder and faster—anything to increase your odds.

The AI industry, after all, is built on a historic bet: of marshaling as much human knowledge and capital as possible to conjure an alien intelligence greater than our own. Everything we’ve seen from Silicon Valley’s leaders in recent months—the legitimate safety fears, the people willing to cast all morality aside to defend Huang—is the result of this bet. The model-collapse behavior is its own form of recursive self-destruction: AI companies are building the very thing they fear; safety obsessives are alienating themselves from the public who could help them tackle an extraordinary collective-action problem.

This is what happens when the bet becomes so big—when the industry is so full of financial, geopolitical, and existential risk—that it creates its own warped logic. It transforms human innovation from a worthy ambition to an inexorable force and, finally, into something akin to a hostage situation. To stop now, Silcon Valley’s leaders argue, would mean losing not merely the future, but also the present. We’re committed to whatever happens next; nothing is more important than driving forward, and no price is too steep.

This is the lie the gambler tells himself. But how can we accept the premise when the logic behind it is degraded? I don’t doubt the power or even the potential of what many in Silicon Valley are building. But this is an industry that is asking for an unprecedented level of trust—trust it has neither earned nor seems all that interested in cultivating. At least for now, humans still have a right to self-determination and are under no obligation to submit to an ideology that might remove our agency without our consent. No vision of the future, no matter how well capitalized it is, is inevitable. Silicon Valley must widen the aperture. Its leaders must broaden the conversation around what this future might look like, what we will value, and how to keep it human.

title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
summary: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permitsEnvironmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.The ba...
content:
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
summary: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA findsOne in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not ...
content:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Continue reading...

title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
summary: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in GazaFears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myan...
content:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Continue reading...

title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
summary: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loansThe European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.The charge rela...
content:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

Continue reading...

title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
summary: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face lega...
content:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
